<task id="ses_efc95de68ffeJ4qGhaNMdCPhWk" state="completed">
<task_result>
## Recommendation

**Use Resend Free over its HTTP API as the practical default**, provided total traffic stays below **100 recipient-emails/day and 3,000/month**. It has the same $0 incremental service cost as your existing Workspace mailbox, with simpler unattended credentials and delivery/bounce reporting.

**Choose the existing dedicated Workspace mailbox + Gmail API instead** if you need more daily capacity, want mail to originate from an actual organization account, or cannot accommodate third-party mail posting to the admin Google Group. Use a separate, non-admin mailbox authorized only for `gmail.send`.

Two issues prevent an unconditional “entirely free” recommendation:

1. **Nonprofit status does not automatically establish Vercel Hobby eligibility.**
2. **Google’s current official docs still conflict about delegated-admin user creation.**

*Checked against official documentation on October 3, 2026. Live service docs take precedence over older Context7 excerpts where they differ.*

## 1. Outbound email: factual comparison

| | Existing Workspace mailbox — Gmail API | Resend Free |
|---|---|---|
| Incremental cost | Standard API usage has no additional cost; mailbox already exists | $0/month |
| Main sending allowance | Normally **2,000 messages/user per rolling 24 hours**; trials have lower limits | **100 recipient-emails per UTC day; 3,000/month** |
| Additional recipient limits | **10,000 total recipients/day; 3,000 external recipients/day; 3,000 unique recipients/day, including at most 2,000 external** | Each `To`, `Cc`, and `Bcc` recipient counts separately |
| Per-message recipients | **500** through Gmail API | Governed by Resend API limits; recipient counting still applies |
| Unattended credential | OAuth refresh token obtained through initial interactive authorization | Server-side API key |
| Sender setup | Gmail-enabled Workspace user; primary address or appropriately configured sending alias | DNS-verified owned domain/subdomain; no Workspace mailbox required for the sender |
| Delivery visibility | API acceptance; bounce messages arrive in the mailbox. `gmail.send` cannot read them | Delivery/bounce events, dashboard and webhooks; **30-day email-data retention** |
| Operational complication | Token revocation, password changes and Workspace policies can require reconnection | Hard free-tier daily/monthly capacity; public signup can exhaust it |

Sources: [Workspace sending limits](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/gmail/gmail-sending-limits-in-google-workspace), [Gmail API scopes](https://developers.google.com/workspace/gmail/api/auth/scopes), [Resend quotas](https://resend.com/docs/knowledge-base/account-quotas-and-limits), [verified domains](https://resend.com/docs/dashboard/domains/introduction).

### Gmail API quotas are separate from mailbox sending limits

The current Gmail API documentation lists:

- **1,200,000 quota units/minute/project**
- **6,000 quota units/minute/user/project**
- `messages.send`: **100 units/request**

That gives approximately **60 send requests/minute for one mailbox**, before other API activity and mailbox limits. Older projects may retain previous quotas; consult the project’s actual quota settings.

It also lists an **80,000,000-unit daily project billing threshold**. Standard use remains free; Google says over-threshold charging details will be announced later in 2026 with at least 90 days’ notice. This is not material to a small signup app, but “Gmail API is permanently unlimited and free” would be inaccurate. [Official quota and pricing documentation](https://developers.google.com/workspace/gmail/api/reference/quota).

### Count the complete signup workflow

Budget verification emails, resends, approval/rejection/expiry outcomes, and admin notifications together.

For example, **one verification + one outcome + one admin notification = three recipient-emails per signup**. Resend’s daily allowance then supports about **33 such complete flows/day**, before retries or other mail. Separate notifications to several admins consume additional quota; a single Google Group address is one addressed recipient at submission.

Resend’s current Free plan includes **three verified domains**. Its next transactional tier starts at **$20/month for 50,000 emails**, without the Free daily cap. [Current pricing](https://resend.com/pricing).

## 2. Can Gmail run unattended with internal OAuth?

**Yes, after initial interactive authorization; it does not require the mailbox owner to remain signed in.**

For the dedicated sender:

- Use `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/gmail.send`, classified as **sensitive**, rather than broader mailbox-reading scopes.
- Obtain offline access with `access_type=offline`; retain the refresh token securely server-side.
- Reauthorization may be necessary if an earlier grant did not produce a refresh token.
- An **Internal** OAuth app must belong to the Workspace/Cloud Identity organization. Internal use does **not** require Google’s public sensitive-scope verification, although Workspace administrators can block or restrict it.

Your public email-verification signup does not itself require Google OAuth. Keep the organization-only Google integration limited to the sender mailbox and acting admins.

Sources: [offline authorization](https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2/web-server#offline), [internal-use verification exception](https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2/production-readiness/sensitive-scope-verification#exceptions), [OAuth configuration behavior](https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2/production-readiness/overview).

**Offline does not mean permanently valid.** Refresh tokens can stop working after revocation, six months without use, a password change when Gmail scopes are present, token-count limits, or administrator policy changes. The well-known **seven-day expiry applies to External apps in Testing requesting these scopes**, not an ordinary Internal configuration. [Refresh-token expiration rules](https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2#expiration).

Keep this mailbox credential independent of the acting admin’s Directory credential: notifications should not depend on an admin currently being logged in.

### Gmail SMTP alternative

It is supported, but is my third choice:

- `smtp.gmail.com`, **465 with TLS/SSL** or **587 with STARTTLS**
- Full mailbox address plus an **app password**, where available
- 2-Step Verification required; organizational policy, security-key-only configuration or Advanced Protection can make app passwords unavailable
- Password changes revoke app passwords
- An app password lacks the explicit send-only permission boundary of `gmail.send`

Google still documents app-password SMTP even though ordinary username/account-password access has been retired. [Workspace SMTP instructions](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/gmail/send-email-from-a-printer-scanner-or-app), [app-password requirements](https://support.google.com/accounts/answer/185833).

Vercel allows outbound **465/587**, blocks **25**, and recommends HTTP APIs over stateful SMTP connections. SMTP must complete within the function lifecycle. [Vercel email guidance](https://vercel.com/kb/guide/sending-emails-from-an-application-on-vercel).

## 3. Vercel Hobby: nonprofit eligibility and capacity

### Eligibility is conditional

Vercel restricts Hobby to **non-commercial personal use**. Its commercial definition includes financial gain for anyone involved in producing the deployment, explicitly including a **paid employee or consultant writing the code**.

It also explicitly says **asking for donations is not commercial usage**.

Therefore:

- A donation-supported, unpaid volunteer project is not automatically disqualified by donations.
- A nonprofit project developed or maintained for payment can fall under the commercial definition.
- Nonprofit registration alone does not resolve the additional “personal use” condition for an organization-operated administration app.

**Confirm Hobby eligibility with Vercel for this specific operation if organizational ownership or paid work is involved.** The docs do not provide a blanket nonprofit exemption. [Fair-use policy](https://vercel.com/docs/limits/fair-use-guidelines#commercial-usage).

### Relevant current Hobby allowances

| Resource | Included allowance |
|---|---:|
| Function invocations | 1 million/month |
| Active CPU | 4 CPU-hours/month |
| Provisioned memory | 360 GB-hours/month |
| Fast data transfer | 100 GB/month |
| Fast origin transfer | 10 GB/month |
| Function maximum duration with Fluid compute | 300 seconds |
| Runtime-log retention | 1 hour |

Most exceeded Hobby allowances require waiting until **30 days have passed** before the affected feature becomes usable again. That is a usage-pause rule, not a 30-day deployment expiration. [Hobby documentation](https://vercel.com/docs/plans/hobby).

### Cron and 30-day request expiry

Current limits are **100 cron jobs/project**, with **each Hobby job running at most once/day**. Execution can occur anywhere within the scheduled hour. Cron delivery is best effort, can be missed or duplicated, and failed invocations are **not automatically retried**. [Cron limits](https://vercel.com/docs/cron-jobs/usage-and-pricing), [delivery behavior](https://vercel.com/docs/cron-jobs/manage-cron-jobs).

For **pending requests expiring after 30 days**, daily cleanup is sufficient if:

- expiry is enforced from the stored timestamp whenever someone views or acts on the request;
- cron handles cleanup and expiry notifications.

A daily job alone cannot guarantee rejection exactly at the 30-day boundary. Notification timing may lag until the next successful run.

## 4. Neon Free: current PostgreSQL capacities

The **live Neon plan page now lists 1 GB/project**, superseding older cached 0.5 GB figures.

| Resource | Current Free allowance |
|---|---:|
| Projects | 100 |
| Branches | 10/project |
| PostgreSQL storage | **1 GB/project; 20 GB total across Free projects** |
| Compute | **100 CU-hours/project/month** |
| Maximum autoscaling | 2 CU, approximately 8 GB RAM |
| Public network transfer | 5 GB/project/month |
| Scale to zero | After 5 minutes idle; cannot disable |
| Point-in-time restore history | **6 hours**, capped change-history allowance |
| Manual snapshots | 1 |
| Scheduled snapshots | Unavailable on Free |
| Monitoring history | 1 day |
| Uptime SLA | None |

[Official plan comparison and enforcement rules](https://neon.com/docs/introduction/plans).

Important practical limits:

- **100 CU-hours is not 100 clock-hours.** At 0.25 CU it permits about **400 active hours/month**; suspended time does not count. A continuously active 0.25 CU database exceeds that allowance.
- All branch computes count toward the project’s compute usage. Frequent polling can prevent the intended idle savings.
- Reactivation adds latency; Neon describes typical wake-up as a few hundred milliseconds. [Scale-to-zero docs](https://neon.com/docs/introduction/scale-to-zero).
- Exhausted compute or transfer suspends compute until the next billing period or upgrade. Storage limits cause storage-increasing operations to fail; the docs explicitly include inserts, updates and deletes. These limits do not delete the data.
- **Six-hour restore history is not a 30-day backup.** Instant restore applies to root branches. Snapshot docs also list post-snapshot-restore PITR limitations. [Backup and restore](https://neon.com/docs/guides/backup-restore).
- Snapshot availability should not be confused with guaranteed zero-cost snapshot storage: current docs publish **$0.09/GB-month** snapshot storage pricing without clearly explaining the Free-plan billing interaction.

Neon Free is plausible for a small requests/audit database, but neither Drizzle nor low visitor traffic removes these capacity and recovery constraints.

## 5. Acting-admin Directory writes: conflict remains unresolved

The current official sources say contradictory things:

- [Administrator privilege definitions](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/users/administrator-privilege-definitions): **Users → Create** is delegable, and the section explicitly says these privileges grant permissions for those operations through the **Directory API**.
- [Directory `User` reference — `isDelegatedAdmin`](https://developers.google.com/workspace/admin/directory/reference/rest/v1/users): delegated administrators **“cannot create or undelete users, or make users administrators.”**
- [`users.insert`](https://developers.google.com/workspace/admin/directory/reference/rest/v1/users/insert): requires `admin.directory.user`, but does not reconcile the privilege contradiction.

**The current docs do not resolve delegated-admin API creation.** Do not claim either universal delegated-admin support or that the contradictory reference is obsolete.

For a docs-backed launch assumption, require an **acting super admin for user creation**, unless Google provides authoritative clarification for delegated admins. Whether you accept that requirement is a product blocker. Other writes still require the acting account’s applicable privileges and scope.

The requested boundary remains sound: public signup verifies email; ordinary self-service creates an approval request; approval authorizes the operation; the Directory write executes with the **acting admin’s OAuth identity**. Notification recipients grant no authority.

## 6. Admin notifications and Google Groups

Use a configured default notification address, editable by an authorized app admin: either a mailbox or Google Group. **Treat it solely as routing configuration**, without inferring app roles or Google permissions from its membership.

For Group delivery:

- Enable email posting.
- Permit the sender under **Who can post**.
- Account for message moderation and spam handling.
- Ensure intended recipients receive individual email rather than only digests/no email.

**Gmail API from an actual same-organization mailbox avoids the external-sender issue, but same-organization status does not bypass members-only posting or moderation.** Add the sender to the group when posting is restricted to members.

For Resend, do not assume a same-domain `From` address guarantees acceptance as an internal Workspace sender. Plan for third-party/external posting restrictions. Google distinguishes **external membership** from **incoming external email**: a private, internal-members-only group can permit external email without becoming publicly readable.

Sources: [organization-wide Group policy](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/groups/set-organization-wide-policies-for-using-groups), [external-email troubleshooting](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/support/troubleshooting/fix-common-issues-with-group-settings), [posting settings](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/groups/about-the-new-groups-release).

## Decisions needed

1. **Vercel eligibility:** unpaid volunteer/personal use, or an organization operation involving paid development?
2. **Email:** stay comfortably below Resend’s 100/day cap, or use the existing Gmail mailbox and accept reconnect maintenance?
3. **User creation:** can a super admin act on creation requests while Google’s delegated-admin documentation remains contradictory?
4. **Notification destination:** which default address/group, and can its posting settings admit the chosen sender?
5. **Recovery:** is six-hour Neon restore history acceptable, or do you need longer independently retained backups?
</task_result>
</task>

parts.text:
Vercel and Neon Free are recorded in the hosting ADR. Administrator email notifications are included.

For email, **a dedicated Workspace mailbox using Gmail’s send-only API permission** is a good fit: no additional email service, organization-owned sending, and no Directory privileges for the sender. It requires a one-time OAuth connection and occasional reconnection if authorization is revoked. [Google documentation](https://developers.google.com/workspace/gmail/api/auth/scopes)

## Round 4 — notifications and operating limits

❓ **Q17 — Email sender:** May the application use a dedicated Workspace mailbox, such as `notifications@your-domain`, for verification, outcome, and administrator notification emails?

➡️ **Recommend:** Yes, with only `gmail.send` permission. Keep its credentials separate from administrators’ Directory credentials.

---

❓ **Q18 — Administrator notifications:** Where should review notifications go, and what should they contain?

➡️ **Recommend:** One configured Google Group, such as `workspace-reviewers@your-domain`. Notify it when a verified signup or profile change request is submitted, with a link to the review queue and minimal personal information. Group membership controls notification delivery only; Google administrative privileges still control approval.

---

❓ **Q19 — Cost ceiling:** If free allowances are exhausted, should the application wait for them to reset, or may it move to a paid plan?

Vercel’s Hobby plan has eligibility restrictions; nonprofit status alone does not establish eligibility. [Vercel policy](https://vercel.com/docs/limits/fair-use-guidelines#commercial-usage)

➡️ **Recommend:** No automatic paid upgrades. Use an eligible Vercel plan and Neon Free; require an explicit budget decision before incurring recurring charges. Surface capacity failures clearly rather than losing submitted requests.

---

❓ **Q20 — Recovery of application records:** Google holds the managed accounts and profiles, but pending requests and approval records live in Neon. Is Neon Free’s native recovery sufficient initially, or do you require longer independent backups?

➡️ **Recommend:** Start with Neon’s native recovery for this small project, accepting its currently documented six-hour restore window. Add independent backups if losing pending workflow records would be unacceptable. [Neon plans](https://neon.com/docs/introduction/plans)

---

One implementation check remains: Google’s documentation conflicts on delegated administrators creating users through the API. We’ll verify that operation in your Workspace organization before relying on it; a denied operation must never be retried under a stronger administrator’s credentials.

Q19: No need to take care of tier management, it will handled manually. The free constraints only mean that the application architecture should be cost effective.
Else: accept recommendations

parts.text:
Understood: **cost-effective architecture; hosting tiers are managed manually outside the application.** The decision documents are updated, and formatting checks pass.

## Shared design

### Onboarding
- Applicants submit given name, family name, verified contact email, and optional phone.
- No personal Google account or applicant dashboard is required.
- Workspace email suggestions are generated programmatically for administrator review; applicants cannot choose an address.
- An authorized administrator accepts or rejects the request.
- Acceptance creates the Workspace account and any explicitly selected group memberships. Membership defaults to **member**; manager/owner assignments are explicit.
- First-login handover uses Google’s Admin console password-reset email flow.
- Rejected requests are deleted after outcome notification. Unreviewed requests expire after 30 days.
- Successful applicant form data is removed after provisioning and handover, retaining only the minimal provisioning record.

### User self-service
- Workspace users sign in through Google and see only their own information.
- Users propose contact email/phone changes; replacement contact emails require verification.
- One pending change request per user; a new submission replaces it.
- An authorized administrator approves or rejects the whole request. Google’s profile changes only after a successful approved write.
- Names, Workspace email, organizational assignments, security settings, and memberships remain administrator-controlled.

### Administration and authority
- Administrators list, edit, suspend, and delete users within their Google privileges.
- They manage groups and direct memberships, including **member, manager, and owner** roles.
- Administrative writes use the acting administrator’s OAuth credentials. Google remains the authority for permissions.
- Suspension is the normal offboarding action. Deletion requires explicit confirmation after data disposition is handled in Google’s Admin console.
- No application-owned administrator roles or domain-wide delegation initially.

### Platform and notifications
- Existing shadcn/Tailwind UI, Next.js on Vercel, Neon Free Postgres through Drizzle.
- Google is authoritative for managed profiles and groups; the database holds application workflows.
- A dedicated Workspace mailbox with `gmail.send` sends verification, outcome, and review notifications.
- A configured Google Group receives review notifications; its membership grants no application privileges.
- Neon’s native recovery is sufficient initially. No application tier-management feature.

The remaining Google integration checks—particularly delegated-admin account creation—will be verified during implementation.

**Does this capture our shared understanding, so I can finalize it as an implementation-ready GitHub specification?**
lgtm

- **Claim**: `gh issue edit <n> --add-assignee @me`, the session's first write.
- **Resolve**: `gh issue comment <n> --body "<answer>"`, then `gh issue close <n>`, then append a context pointer (gist + link) to the map's Decisions-so-far.

parts.text: I’m publishing the agreed design as a GitHub specification. I’m also checking one implementation detail: ordinary users’ Directory reads can omit private fields, so displaying their full contact profile may need a separate read-only Google authorization. Administrative writes will still use the acting administrator’s credentials.

input.prompt: Research only Google official documentation. Finalizing spec nonprofit Google Workspace selfservice app. Ordinary users sign in own profile and request email phone changes admin approve own OAuth Directory updates no DWD. Need determine nonadmin Directory users.get viewType domain_public own profile includes private emails[] phones[]? Full accessible self? Existing docs non-admin public and only admins modify. Confirm secure straightforward separate OAuth read-only directory connection from custom admin Users Read with admin.directory.user.readonly for nonadmin authenticated own-profile display, no shared write credentials; is Users Read enough and OU scope honored? Avoid People API source-of-truth divergence unless explicit mirrored admin Directory contacts. Return short facts official URLs and recommendation. No edits.

state.output:
<task id="ses_efc8e61acffeW7ninIFn7NzlFx" state="completed">
<task_result>
**Yes: a separate, server-side read-only admin Directory connection is the straightforward solution for displaying private Directory data to ordinary users. Their own OAuth token does not provide full self-access.**

### Confirmed facts — Google official documentation

- **Non-admin access is public-only, including when requesting oneself.** Google documents `users.get` / `users.list` with `viewType=domain_public` for non-admins. That view includes only fields visible to other domain users; **no self exception is documented**. `projection=FULL` does not override visibility. Contact sharing must be enabled, and hidden users are excluded.  
  [Non-admin retrieval](https://developers.google.com/workspace/admin/directory/v1/guides/manage-users#retrieve_users_non_admin) · [View/projection definitions](https://developers.google.com/workspace/admin/directory/reference/rest/v1/users/get)

- **Do not promise complete private `emails[]` / `phones[]` through `domain_public`.** Publicly exposed information may be available, but administrator-only information is outside that view. Also, `home` is a contact **type**, not a privacy flag: the documented arrays have no per-entry visibility property. Recovery details are separate `recoveryEmail` / `recoveryPhone` fields.  
  [User resource](https://developers.google.com/workspace/admin/directory/reference/rest/v1/users)

- **Users → Read plus `admin.directory.user.readonly` is sufficient for user-resource reads.** Google explicitly maps the Users privileges to Directory API operations, and `users.get` accepts that OAuth scope. Use `viewType=admin_view`; no Users Update privilege or write scope is required for this read connection.  
  [Users privileges](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/users/administrator-privilege-definitions#users) · [users.get](https://developers.google.com/workspace/admin/directory/reference/rest/v1/users/get)

- **Users privileges support OU-scoped role assignments.** Google documents restricting these administrative actions to selected OUs, including roles used for API operations. The OAuth scope does not enlarge the account’s role permissions. **OU scope is not an own-profile restriction**; your backend must enforce that separately.  
  [OU-scoped roles](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/users/create-an-admin-role-for-an-organizational-unit) · [Privilege definitions](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/users/administrator-privilege-definitions#users)

- **Writes require admin authority and `admin.directory.user`.** Approval itself is your application’s workflow. `users.update` replaces supplied arrays as a whole, so preserve unaffected email/phone entries.  
  [users.update](https://developers.google.com/workspace/admin/directory/reference/rest/v1/users/update)

### Recommendation for the spec

Use ordinary Google sign-in, then a backend-only Directory reader authorized by a **dedicated delegated admin with Users → Read**, scoped to the relevant OUs. Bind each profile request to the authenticated user’s server-resolved Directory identity; never accept an arbitrary target from the browser. Keep this reader’s tokens separate from approvers’ personal OAuth write tokens. **No DWD is needed.**

For strong read/write isolation, use a separate OAuth project for the reader: Google’s incremental authorization can combine grants across different clients within one project. [OAuth grant behavior](https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2/web-server#incrementalAuth)

Keep Directory authoritative. People API returns merged profile/contact sources and is not documented as an exact replacement for the admin Directory record; use it only with an explicitly defined mirror/source mapping. [People API sources](https://developers.google.com/people#merged-view)
</task_result>
</task>

input.command:
gh label create ready-for-agent --description "Fully specified, ready for an agent to implement" --color 0E8A16 && gh issue create --repo itsmeyaw/binden --title "Google Workspace onboarding, self-service, and administration" --label enhancement --label ready-for-agent --body '## Goal
Build a small nonprofit self-service management application for one Google Workspace organization. Google is authoritative for managed accounts, current profiles, groups, and administrative permissions. The approved design targets inexpensive operation using the existing Next.js, shadcn/Tailwind, and Drizzle setup, Vercel hosting, and Neon Free Postgres. Hosting tiers are managed manually outside the application.

## Domain language
- Applicant: a person requesting a managed Workspace account.
- Signup request: applicant information awaiting administrator review; not an existing Workspace user.
- Workspace user: a person with an existing managed Google account.
- Administrator: a Workspace user whose actual Google privileges authorize the requested action.
- Contact email: an external/reachable contact address, distinct from Workspace primary email, aliases, and account recovery email.
- Profile change request: proposed contact email/phone changes awaiting approval.
- Suspension: reversible account deactivation retaining data. Deletion is account removal after data disposition.
- Group member, manager, and owner: Google Group membership roles, not application administrator roles.

## Approved onboarding workflow
1. Public signup requires given name, family name, and verified contact email; phone is optional. A personal Google account is not required. No applicant dashboard.
2. Submitted, verified requests appear in the administrator review queue and trigger an email notification.
3. Generate Workspace email suggestions programmatically using a given.family convention. Applicants cannot choose an address. The reviewing administrator confirms or edits the suggestion. Check availability in Google; never associate an applicant with an existing account merely because an address collides.
4. An authorized administrator accepts or rejects the request. Acceptance provisions the account through Google using the acting administrator OAuth credentials.
5. Initial groups are optional, explicitly selected, and default to member. Manager/owner assignments require explicit selection and sufficient authority. No automatic memberships.
6. Provision with a random temporary password and required password change. Complete handover manually using the Google Admin console existing-user password reset and email flow. Never email plaintext passwords or retain them in application records/logs.
7. Send outcomes to the verified contact email. Delete rejected request data after notification. Expire unreviewed requests after 30 days. Remove successful applicant form data after provisioning and handover; retain only a minimal provisioning record identifying the resulting Google account and approving administrator.
8. Failed or partially completed provisioning must remain recoverable. Retrying must not create duplicate accounts or lose the request. Account creation, membership assignment, and handover are distinct completion steps.

## Approved self-service workflow
1. Existing Workspace users sign in through Google. Enforce organizational membership from verified Google identity, not an email suffix or client hint. Resolve a stable Directory identity server-side and handle email changes safely; do not assume undocumented equality between OIDC sub and Directory User.id.
2. A user can see only their own permitted profile and their own request. All ownership checks are enforced server-side.
3. Name changes, Workspace email, organizational assignments, group membership, account status, account recovery, and security settings are administrator-controlled.
4. Users submit contact email/phone changes for approval. Verify a replacement contact email before it can be approved. Do not write submitted values into Google immediately.
5. Each user has at most one pending request; a newer submission replaces it. An administrator approves/rejects the whole request. An approval must apply the reviewed version, not a replacement submitted concurrently.
6. Approved changes execute with the approving administrator OAuth credentials and actual Google privileges. Preserve unrelated Google email/phone array entries. Store contact details in emails[]/phones[], not primaryEmail or recovery fields.
7. Google remains the current-profile authority. Pending proposals and verification evidence are workflow data, not a mirrored authoritative user table.

## Google access and authorization
- No domain-wide delegation initially. Ordinary-user consent does not grant Directory write authority.
- Administrative writes use the acting administrator token, never a stronger shared account. Google must enforce action/resource/OU restrictions. Do not authorize from isAdmin/isDelegatedAdmin alone or a local role table. Never retry a permission denial using stronger credentials.
- Relevant write scopes are admin.directory.user and admin.directory.group. Request rolemanagement.readonly only if role inspection is needed and authorized. Respect indirect role assignments and scope when interpreting roles.
- Ordinary-user Directory reads are domain-public only, without documented full self-access. Provide own-profile display through an isolated backend read-only OAuth connection authorized by a delegated account with Users Read in applicable OUs and admin.directory.user.readonly. Derive its target from the session; reject arbitrary target identifiers. Return only permitted own-profile data. Keep the reader isolated from write grants.
- Keep OAuth credentials server-side and isolated by purpose. Handle revocation/reconnection explicitly. Recheck active user state for protected access so an existing application session does not preserve access after suspension/deletion.

## Administrator capabilities
- List and edit users within actual Google authority; action and resource permissions apply to reads and writes.
- Suspend/unsuspend users. Suspension is the normal offboarding action.
- Delete users only after explicit confirmation that data disposition was resolved manually in Google Admin console. No in-application data-transfer automation initially.
- Create, edit, and delete Google Groups; manage direct Workspace-user memberships with member/manager/owner roles.
- Preserve existing group settings. No nested-group management, external-member management, or posting/privacy settings editor initially. Group ownership does not itself grant application-wide administration.

## Notifications
- Use a dedicated Workspace mailbox with an offline OAuth grant limited to gmail.send; it needs no Directory administrative privileges. Its token is separate from the profile reader and acting administrators.
- Send applicant verification and outcome emails, plus notifications for verified signup/profile change submissions.
- Deliver administrator notifications to one configured Google Group with a review-queue link and minimal personal information. Group membership affects notification delivery only, never approval authority. Configure posting permissions and subscriptions for the sender/recipients.
- Delivery failures must be visible and retryable without duplicating provisioning or losing requests. Do not send verification secrets, passwords, or full submitted profiles to the notification group.

## Platform and operational boundaries
- Use the existing preconfigured shadcn/Tailwind UI, accessible forms, Next.js App Router, and Drizzle ORM.
- Deploy on Vercel with Neon Free Postgres. Favor serverless/on-demand work and idle database scale-to-zero; avoid continuous polling or always-on infrastructure.
- No application tier management, quota-based upgrades, or billing system. Provider plan handling is manual.
- Start with Neon native recovery, accepting the currently documented six-hour Free restore window. Independent backups are deferred.
- Enforce request expiration when reading/acting; scheduled cleanup can run daily. Cleanup/retries must tolerate duplicate or missed invocations.
- Validate public input and rate-limit email-verification/public submissions to prevent quota exhaustion. Do not lose submissions on provider or quota failures.
- Persist only necessary workflow, verification, minimal operational records, and protected credentials/session data. Do not mirror current Google profiles or create application-owned admin roles.

## Integration checks before shipping
- Google docs conflict on delegated-admin users.insert support. Verify creation with the intended custom role in the actual Workspace tenant before relying on it. If denied, an appropriately privileged administrator must perform approval; do not escalate silently.
- Verify own-profile private contact reads through the isolated reader, organizational restrictions, and role/OU-scoped admin access.
- Verify member/manager/owner changes; manager requires Groups for Business support.
- Verify existing-user Console reset-email handover and notification Group delivery.

## Acceptance checks
- An unverified or invalid signup cannot enter the review queue.
- Applicants cannot select Workspace email or provision themselves.
- Repeated approval/retry cannot create a duplicate account.
- Ordinary users cannot read another profile/request or write Directory fields directly.
- A replaced profile request cannot be approved under stale reviewed contents.
- Unauthorized administrator operations fail without fallback credentials.
- Approved contact changes preserve unrelated Directory entries and recovery settings.
- Google-side role changes, suspension, and deletion are respected by protected application access.
- Group role changes, request outcomes, expiry, handover, and email failures follow the workflows above.
- Required lint/format/build checks and meaningful authorization/workflow checks pass.

## Development workflow
Implement in .worktrees using the repository stacked-PR workflow. Read installed Next.js guides before coding. Keep the existing UI patterns, use Drizzle, and review for correctness and minimum necessary complexity.

## Official references
- Directory users and non-admin access: https://developers.google.com/workspace/admin/directory/v1/guides/manage-users
- User read views: https://developers.google.com/workspace/admin/directory/reference/rest/v1/users/get
- User creation: https://developers.google.com/workspace/admin/directory/reference/rest/v1/users/insert
- User updates: https://developers.google.com/workspace/admin/directory/reference/rest/v1/users/update
- Administrator privileges: https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/users/administrator-privilege-definitions
- Domain-wide delegation trade-offs: https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/apps/domain-wide-delegation-best-practices
- Console handover: https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/users/reset-a-users-password
- Gmail send-only scope: https://developers.google.com/workspace/gmail/api/auth/scopes
- Neon plans: https://neon.com/docs/introduction/plans

Approved by the project owner after the design interview. This issue is the canonical implementation specification.'

7. Send outcomes to the verified contact email. Delete rejected request data after notification. Expire unreviewed requests after 30 days. Remove successful applicant form data after provisioning and handover; retain only a minimal provisioning record identifying the resulting Google account and approving administrator.
8. Failed or partially completed provisioning must remain recoverable. Retrying must not create duplicate accounts or lose the request. Account creation, membership assignment, and handover are distinct completion steps.

## Approved self-service workflow
1. Existing Workspace users sign in through Google. Enforce organizational membership from verified Google identity, not an email suffix or client hint. Resolve a stable Directory identity server-side and handle email changes safely; do not assume undocumented equality between OIDC sub and Directory User.id.
2. A user can see only their own permitted profile and their own request. All ownership checks are enforced server-side.
3. Name changes, Workspace email, organizational assignments, group membership, account status, account recovery, and security settings are administrator-controlled.
4. Users submit contact email/phone changes for approval. Verify a replacement contact email before it can be approved. Do not write submitted values into Google immediately.
5. Each user has at most one pending request; a newer submission replaces it. An administrator approves/rejects the whole request. An approval must apply the reviewed version, not a replacement submitted concurrently.
6. Approved changes execute with the approving administrator OAuth credentials and actual Google privileges. Preserve unrelated Google email/phone array entries. Store contact details in emails[]/phones[], not primaryEmail or recovery fields.
7. Google remains the current-profile authority. Pending proposals and verification evidence are workflow data, not a mirrored authoritative user table.

## Google access and authorization
- No domain-wide delegation initially. Ordinary-user consent does not grant Directory write authority.
- Administrative writes use the acting administrator token, never a stronger shared account. Google must enforce action/resource/OU restrictions. Do not authorize from isAdmin/isDelegatedAdmin alone or a local role table. Never retry a permission denial using stronger credentials.
- Relevant write scopes are admin.directory.user and admin.directory.group. Request rolemanagement.readonly only if role inspection is needed and authorized. Respect indirect role assignments and scope when interpreting roles.
- Ordinary-user Directory reads are domain-public only, without documented full self-access. Provide own-profile display through an isolated backend read-only OAuth connection authorized by a delegated account with Users Read in applicable OUs and admin.directory.user.readonly. Derive its target from the session; reject arbitrary target identifiers. Return only permitted own-profile data. Keep the reader isolated from write grants.
- Keep OAuth credentials server-side and isolated by purpose. Handle revocation/reconnection explicitly. Recheck active user state for protected access so an existing application session does not preserve access after suspension/deletion.

## Administrator capabilities
- List and edit users within actual Google authority; action and resource permissions apply to reads and writes.
- Suspend/unsuspend users. Suspension is the normal offboarding action.
- Delete users only after explicit confirmation that data disposition was resolved manually in Google Admin console. No in-application data-transfer automation initially.
- Create, edit, and delete Google Groups; manage direct Workspace-user memberships with member/manager/owner roles.
- Preserve existing group settings. No nested-group management, external-member management, or posting/privacy settings editor initially. Group ownership does not itself grant application-wide administration.

## Notifications
- Use a dedicated Workspace mailbox with an offline OAuth grant limited to gmail.send; it needs no Directory administrative privileges. Its token is separate from the profile reader and acting administrators.
- Send applicant verification and outcome emails, plus notifications for verified signup/profile change submissions.
- Deliver administrator notifications to one configured Google Group with a review-queue link and minimal personal information. Group membership affects notification delivery only, never approval authority. Configure posting permissions and subscriptions for the sender/recipients.
- Delivery failures must be visible and retryable without duplicating provisioning or losing requests. Do not send verification secrets, passwords, or full submitted profiles to the notification group.

## Platform and operational boundaries
- Use the existing preconfigured shadcn/Tailwind UI, accessible forms, Next.js App Router, and Drizzle ORM.
- Deploy on Vercel with Neon Free Postgres. Favor serverless/on-demand work and idle database scale-to-zero; avoid continuous polling or always-on infrastructure.
- No application tier management, quota-based upgrades, or billing system. Provider plan handling is manual.
- Start with Neon native recovery, accepting the currently documented six-hour Free restore window. Independent backups are deferred.
- Enforce request expiration when reading/acting; scheduled cleanup can run daily. Cleanup/retries must tolerate duplicate or missed invocations.
- Validate public input and rate-limit email-verification/public submissions to prevent quota exhaustion. Do not lose submissions on provider or quota failures.
- Persist only necessary workflow, verification, minimal operational records, and protected credentials/session data. Do not mirror current Google profiles or create application-owned admin roles.

## Integration checks before shipping
- Google docs conflict on delegated-admin users.insert support. Verify creation with the intended custom role in the actual Workspace tenant before relying on it. If denied, an appropriately privileged administrator must perform approval; do not escalate silently.
- Verify own-profile private contact reads through the isolated reader, organizational restrictions, and role/OU-scoped admin access.
- Verify member/manager/owner changes; manager requires Groups for Business support.
- Verify existing-user Console reset-email handover and notification Group delivery.

## Acceptance checks
- An unverified or invalid signup cannot enter the review queue.
- Applicants cannot select Workspace email or provision themselves.
- Repeated approval/retry cannot create a duplicate account.
- Ordinary users cannot read another profile/request or write Directory fields directly.
- A replaced profile request cannot be approved under stale reviewed contents.
- Unauthorized administrator operations fail without fallback credentials.
- Approved contact changes preserve unrelated Directory entries and recovery settings.
- Google-side role changes, suspension, and deletion are respected by protected application access.
- Group role changes, request outcomes, expiry, handover, and email failures follow the workflows above.
- Required lint/format/build checks and meaningful authorization/workflow checks pass.

## Development workflow
Implement in .worktrees using the repository stacked-PR workflow. Read installed Next.js guides before coding. Keep the existing UI patterns, use Drizzle, and review for correctness and minimum necessary complexity.

## Official references
- Directory users and non-admin access: https://developers.google.com/workspace/admin/directory/v1/guides/manage-users
- User read views: https://developers.google.com/workspace/admin/directory/reference/rest/v1/users/get
- User creation: https://developers.google.com/workspace/admin/directory/reference/rest/v1/users/insert
- User updates: https://developers.google.com/workspace/admin/directory/reference/rest/v1/users/update
- Administrator privileges: https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/users/administrator-privilege-definitions
- Domain-wide delegation trade-offs: https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/apps/domain-wide-delegation-best-practices
- Console handover: https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/users/reset-a-users-password
- Gmail send-only scope: https://developers.google.com/workspace/gmail/api/auth/scopes
- Neon plans: https://neon.com/docs/introduction/plans

<skill_content name="codebase-design">
# Skill: codebase-design

# Codebase Design

Design **deep modules**: a lot of behaviour behind a small interface, placed at a clean seam, testable through that interface. Use this language and these principles wherever code is being designed or restructured. The aim is leverage for callers, locality for maintainers, and testability for everyone.

## Glossary

Use these terms exactly: don't substitute "component," "service," "API," or "boundary." Consistent language is the whole point.

**Module**: anything with an interface and an implementation. Deliberately scale-agnostic: a function, class, package, or tier-spanning slice. _Avoid_: unit, component, service.

**Interface**: everything a caller must know to use the module correctly: the type signature, but also invariants, ordering constraints, error modes, required configuration, and performance characteristics. _Avoid_: API, signature (too narrow, they refer only to the type-level surface).

**Implementation**: what's inside a module, its body of code. Distinct from **Adapter**: a thing can be a small adapter with a large implementation (a Postgres repo) or a large adapter with a small implementation (an in-memory fake). Reach for "adapter" when the seam is the topic; "implementation" otherwise.

**Depth**: leverage at the interface. The amount of behaviour a caller (or test) can exercise per unit of interface they have to learn. A module is **deep** when a large amount of behaviour sits behind a small interface, **shallow** when the interface is nearly as complex as the implementation.

**Seam** _(Michael Feathers)_: a place where you can alter behaviour without editing in that place; the *location* at which a module's interface lives. Where to put the seam is its own design decision, distinct from what goes behind it. _Avoid_: boundary (overloaded with DDD's bounded context).

**Adapter**: a concrete thing that satisfies an interface at a seam. Describes *role* (what slot it fills), not substance (what's inside).

**Leverage**: what callers get from depth. More capability per unit of interface they learn. One implementation pays back across N call sites and M tests.

**Locality**: what maintainers get from depth. Change, bugs, knowledge, and verification concentrate in one place rather than spreading across callers. Fix once, fixed everywhere.

## Deep vs shallow

**Deep module** = small interface + lots of implementation:

```
┌─────────────────────┐
│   Small Interface   │  ← Few methods, simple params
├─────────────────────┤
│                     │
│  Deep Implementation│  ← Complex logic hidden
│                     │
└─────────────────────┘
```

**Shallow module** = large interface + little implementation (avoid):

```
┌─────────────────────────────────┐
│       Large Interface           │  ← Many methods, complex params
├─────────────────────────────────┤
│  Thin Implementation            │  ← Just passes through
└─────────────────────────────────┘
```

When designing an interface, ask:

- Can I reduce the number of methods?
- Can I simplify the parameters?
- Can I hide more complexity inside?

## Principles

- **Depth is a property of the interface, not the implementation.** A deep module can be internally composed of small, mockable, swappable parts; they just aren't part of the interface. A module can have **internal seams** (private to its implementation, used by its own tests) as well as the **external seam** at its interface.
- **The deletion test.** Imagine deleting the module. If complexity vanishes, it was a pass-through. If complexity reappears across N callers, it was earning its keep.
- **The interface is the test surface.** Callers and tests cross the same seam. If you want to test *past* the interface, the module is probably the wrong shape.
- **One adapter means a hypothetical seam. Two adapters means a real one.** Don't introduce a seam unless something actually varies across it.

## Designing for testability

Good interfaces make testing natural:

1. **Accept dependencies, don't create them.**

   ```typescript
   // Testable
   function processOrder(order, paymentGateway) {}

   // Hard to test
   function processOrder(order) {
     const gateway = new StripeGateway();
   }
   ```

2. **Return results, don't produce side effects.**

   ```typescript
   // Testable
   function calculateDiscount(cart): Discount {}

   // Hard to test
   function applyDiscount(cart): void {
     cart.total -= discount;
   }
   ```

3. **Small surface area.** Fewer methods = fewer tests needed. Fewer params = simpler test setup.

## Relationships

- A **Module** has exactly one **Interface** (the surface it presents to callers and tests).
- **Depth** is a property of a **Module**, measured against its **Interface**.
- A **Seam** is where a **Module**'s **Interface** lives.
- An **Adapter** sits at a **Seam** and satisfies the **Interface**.
- **Depth** produces **Leverage** for callers and **Locality** for maintainers.

## Rejected framings

- **Depth as ratio of implementation-lines to interface-lines** (Ousterhout): rewards padding the implementation. We use depth-as-leverage instead.
- **"Interface" as the TypeScript `interface` keyword or a class's public methods**: too narrow: interface here includes every fact a caller must know.
- **"Boundary"**: overloaded with DDD's bounded context. Say **seam** or **interface**.

## Going deeper

- **Deepening a cluster given its dependencies**, see [DEEPENING.md](DEEPENING.md): dependency categories, seam discipline, and replace-don't-layer testing.
- **Exploring alternative interfaces**, see [DESIGN-IT-TWICE.md](DESIGN-IT-TWICE.md): spin up parallel sub-agents to design the interface several radically different ways, then compare on depth, locality, and seam placement.

_Avoid_: User, pending user

An applicant's submitted information awaiting an administrator's acceptance or rejection.
_Avoid_: Account, pending user

A Google Group within the nonprofit's Workspace organization.

A Workspace user's relationship to a group, with a member, manager, or owner role.

A group member with Google's owner role in that group; this role does not itself confer application administrator authority.

**Initial group membership**:
A group membership explicitly selected by the reviewing administrator during onboarding, with no automatic assignments. Its role is member unless manager or owner is explicitly selected.

1: # Use administrator OAuth and approved profile changes
2: 
3: Ordinary-user OAuth consent does not authorize Directory profile writes, even to the user's own account. For this small nonprofit, users submit verified contact email and phone changes for approval; the application executes approved changes and administrative operations using the acting administrator's OAuth credentials. Google therefore enforces that administrator's privileges and resource restrictions, without a shared stronger account or a parallel application role model.
4: 
5: Prefer this workflow over domain-wide delegation: Google's Directory user write scope is not limited to contact fields, and delegation scopes do not restrict which account a service account may impersonate. The trade-off is that contact changes wait for an authorized administrator instead of taking effect immediately. Domain-wide delegation can be reconsidered if that approval delay becomes unacceptable.
6: 
7: Request `admin.directory.user` for user management and `admin.directory.group` for group and membership management; add read-only role inspection only if required for the interface. Restrict profile change requests to contact email and phone, preserve unrelated Directory entries, and keep Workspace email, account recovery fields, and security settings outside that workflow. A new contact email must be verified before it can be approved. Do not retry denied operations using stronger credentials.
8:

# Use administrator OAuth and approved profile changes

Ordinary-user OAuth consent does not authorize Directory profile writes, even to the user's own account. For this small nonprofit, users submit verified contact email and phone changes for approval; the application executes approved changes and administrative operations using the acting administrator's OAuth credentials. Google therefore enforces that administrator's privileges and resource restrictions, without a shared stronger account or a parallel application role model.

Prefer this workflow over domain-wide delegation: Google's Directory user write scope is not limited to contact fields, and delegation scopes do not restrict which account a service account may impersonate. The trade-off is that contact changes wait for an authorized administrator instead of taking effect immediately. Domain-wide delegation can be reconsidered if that approval delay becomes unacceptable.

Request `admin.directory.user` for user management and `admin.directory.group` for group and membership management; add read-only role inspection only if required for the interface. Restrict profile change requests to contact email and phone, preserve unrelated Directory entries, and keep Workspace email, account recovery fields, and security settings outside that workflow. A new contact email must be verified before it can be approved. Do not retry denied operations using stronger credentials.

Send verification, outcome, and administrator notification emails through a dedicated Workspace mailbox with a separate offline OAuth grant limited to `gmail.send`. Notify a configured Google Group when a verified signup or profile change request is submitted, including a review-queue link and minimal personal information. The notification group's membership determines delivery only, never approval authority; configure it to accept mail from the sender.

To display the user's actual contact information, use a separate backend-only OAuth connection with `admin.directory.user.readonly` and a delegated account limited to Users Read in the relevant organizational units. Resolve the target from the authenticated identity and return only that user's permitted profile fields. Keep this reader isolated from write grants; it must not perform administrative or approved-profile writes.

{"body":"## Goal
Build a small nonprofit self-service management application for one Google Workspace organization. Google is authoritative for managed accounts, current profiles, groups, and administrative permissions. The approved design targets inexpensive operation using the existing Next.js, shadcn/Tailwind, and Drizzle setup, Vercel hosting, and Neon Free Postgres. Hosting tiers are managed manually outside the application.

## Domain language
- Applicant: a person requesting a managed Workspace account.
- Signup request: applicant information awaiting administrator review; not an existing Workspace user.
- Workspace user: a person with an existing managed Google account.
- Administrator: a Workspace user whose actual Google privileges authorize the requested action.
- Contact email: an external/reachable contact address, distinct from Workspace primary email, aliases, and account recovery email.
- Profile change request: proposed contact email/phone changes awaiting approval.
- Suspension: reversible account deactivation retaining data. Deletion is account removal after data disposition.
- Group member, manager, and owner: Google Group membership roles, not application administrator roles.

## Approved onboarding workflow
1. Public signup requires given name, family name, and verified contact email; phone is optional. A personal Google account is not required. No applicant dashboard.
2. Submitted, verified requests appear in the administrator review queue and trigger an email notification.
3. Generate Workspace email suggestions programmatically using a given.family convention. Applicants cannot choose an address. The reviewing administrator confirms or edits the suggestion. Check availability in Google; never associate an applicant with an existing account merely because an address collides.
4. An authorized administrator accepts or rejects the request. Acceptance provisions the account through Google using the acting administrator OAuth credentials.
5. Initial groups are optional, explicitly selected, and default to member. Manager/owner assignments require explicit selection and sufficient authority. No automatic memberships.
6. Provision with a random temporary password and required password change. Complete handover manually using the Google Admin console existing-user password reset and email flow. Never email plaintext passwords or retain them in application records/logs.
7. Send outcomes to the verified contact email. Delete rejected request data after notification. Expire unreviewed requests after 30 days. Remove successful applicant form data after provisioning and handover; retain only a minimal provisioning record identifying the resulting Google account and approving administrator.
8. Failed or partially completed provisioning must remain recoverable. Retrying must not create duplicate accounts or lose the request. Account creation, membership assignment, and handover are distinct completion steps.

## Approved self-service workflow
1. Existing Workspace users sign in through Google. Enforce organizational membership from verified Google identity, not an email suffix or client hint. Resolve a stable Directory identity server-side and handle email changes safely; do not assume undocumented equality between OIDC sub and Directory User.id.
2. A user can see only their own permitted profile and their own request. All ownership checks are enforced server-side.
3. Name changes, Workspace email, organizational assignments, group membership, account status, account recovery, and security settings are administrator-controlled.
4. Users submit contact email/phone changes for approval. Verify a replacement contact email before it can be approved. Do not write submitted values into Google immediately.
5. Each user has at most one pending request; a newer submission replaces it. An administrator approves/rejects the whole request. An approval must apply the reviewed version, not a replacement submitted concurrently.
6. Approved changes execute with the approving administrator OAuth credentials and actual Google privileges. Preserve unrelated Google email/phone array entries. Store contact details in emails[]/phones[], not primaryEmail or recovery fields.
7. Google remains the current-profile authority. Pending proposals and verification evidence are workflow data, not a mirrored authoritative user table.

## Google access and authorization
- No domain-wide delegation initially. Ordinary-user consent does not grant Directory write authority.
- Administrative writes use the acting administrator token, never a stronger shared account. Google must enforce action/resource/OU restrictions. Do not authorize from isAdmin/isDelegatedAdmin alone or a local role table. Never retry a permission denial using stronger credentials.
- Relevant write scopes are admin.directory.user and admin.directory.group. Request rolemanagement.readonly only if role inspection is needed and authorized. Respect indirect role assignments and scope when interpreting roles.
- Ordinary-user Directory reads are domain-public only, without documented full self-access. Provide own-profile display through an isolated backend read-only OAuth connection authorized by a delegated account with Users Read in applicable OUs and admin.directory.user.readonly. Derive its target from the session; reject arbitrary target identifiers. Return only permitted own-profile data. Keep the reader isolated from write grants.
- Keep OAuth credentials server-side and isolated by purpose. Handle revocation/reconnection explicitly. Recheck active user state for protected access so an existing application session does not preserve access after suspension/deletion.

## Administrator capabilities
- List and edit users within actual Google authority; action and resource permissions apply to reads and writes.
- Suspend/unsuspend users. Suspension is the normal offboarding action.
- Delete users only after explicit confirmation that data disposition was resolved manually in Google Admin console. No in-application data-transfer automation initially.
- Create, edit, and delete Google Groups; manage direct Workspace-user memberships with member/manager/owner roles.
- Preserve existing group settings. No nested-group management, external-member management, or posting/privacy settings editor initially. Group ownership does not itself grant application-wide administration.

## Notifications
- Use a dedicated Workspace mailbox with an offline OAuth grant limited to gmail.send; it needs no Directory administrative privileges. Its token is separate from the profile reader and acting administrators.
- Send applicant verification and outcome emails, plus notifications for verified signup/profile change submissions.
- Deliver administrator notifications to one configured Google Group with a review-queue link and minimal personal information. Group membership affects notification delivery only, never approval authority. Configure posting permissions and subscriptions for the sender/recipients.
- Delivery failures must be visible and retryable without duplicating provisioning or losing requests. Do not send verification secrets, passwords, or full submitted profiles to the notification group.

## Platform and operational boundaries
- Use the existing preconfigured shadcn/Tailwind UI, accessible forms, Next.js App Router, and Drizzle ORM.
- Deploy on Vercel with Neon Free Postgres. Favor serverless/on-demand work and idle database scale-to-zero; avoid continuous polling or always-on infrastructure.
- No application tier management, quota-based upgrades, or billing system. Provider plan handling is manual.
- Start with Neon native recovery, accepting the currently documented six-hour Free restore window. Independent backups are deferred.
- Enforce request expiration when reading/acting; scheduled cleanup can run daily. Cleanup/retries must tolerate duplicate or missed invocations.
- Validate public input and rate-limit email-verification/public submissions to prevent quota exhaustion. Do not lose submissions on provider or quota failures.
- Persist only necessary workflow, verification, minimal operational records, and protected credentials/session data. Do not mirror current Google profiles or create application-owned admin roles.

## Integration checks before shipping
- Google docs conflict on delegated-admin users.insert support. Verify creation with the intended custom role in the actual Workspace tenant before relying on it. If denied, an appropriately privileged administrator must perform approval; do not escalate silently.
- Verify own-profile private contact reads through the isolated reader, organizational restrictions, and role/OU-scoped admin access.
- Verify member/manager/owner changes; manager requires Groups for Business support.
- Verify existing-user Console reset-email handover and notification Group delivery.

## Acceptance checks
- An unverified or invalid signup cannot enter the review queue.
- Applicants cannot select Workspace email or provision themselves.
- Repeated approval/retry cannot create a duplicate account.
- Ordinary users cannot read another profile/request or write Directory fields directly.
- A replaced profile request cannot be approved under stale reviewed contents.
- Unauthorized administrator operations fail without fallback credentials.
- Approved contact changes preserve unrelated Directory entries and recovery settings.
- Google-side role changes, suspension, and deletion are respected by protected application access.
- Group role changes, request outcomes, expiry, handover, and email failures follow the workflows above.
- Required lint/format/build checks and meaningful authorization/workflow checks pass.

## Development workflow
Implement in .worktrees using the repository stacked-PR workflow. Read installed Next.js guides before coding. Keep the existing UI patterns, use Drizzle, and review for correctness and minimum necessary complexity.

## Official references
- Directory users and non-admin access: https://developers.google.com/workspace/admin/directory/v1/guides/manage-users
- User read views: https://developers.google.com/workspace/admin/directory/reference/rest/v1/users/get
- User creation: https://developers.google.com/workspace/admin/directory/reference/rest/v1/users/insert
- User updates: https://developers.google.com/workspace/admin/directory/reference/rest/v1/users/update
- Administrator privileges: https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/users/administrator-privilege-definitions
- Domain-wide delegation trade-offs: https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/apps/domain-wide-delegation-best-practices
- Console handover: https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/users/reset-a-users-password
- Gmail send-only scope: https://developers.google.com/workspace/gmail/api/auth/scopes
- Neon plans: https://neon.com/docs/introduction/plans

Account handover uses the Admin console's existing-user password reset and email flow, with a required password change, rather than emailing a plaintext password.

Unreviewed signup requests expire after 30 days. Rejected applicant profiles are deleted after outcome notification; successful applicant form data is removed after provisioning and handover. Retain only a minimal operational record identifying the resulting Google account and approving administrator. Email verification evidence and pending workflow data may live in the application without becoming a second source of truth for the current Workspace profile.
